goals.0: Execute-only setuid binary: hook it with LD_PRELOAD and dump its own memory to read the password embedded in .rodata.
goals.1: utumno1 runs any file whose name starts with sh_ in a given directory, executing the filename bytes as code on an RWX page.
goals.2: utumno2 only proceeds when argc==0 (launch it via execve with an empty argv); it then strcpy()s an environment entry over the saved return address.
goals.3: utumno3 reads (index, byte) pairs and writes each byte at a computed stack offset (XORed per iteration) — 8 writes overwrite the return address.
goals.4: utumno4 checks only the low 16 bits of the size argument against 63, then memcpy()s that many bytes into a 0xf000 stack buffer — pass 65536 and overflow.
goals.5: Same argc==0 gate as level 2; hihi() strcpy/strncpy copies envp[10] into a 20-byte buffer and overflows.
goals.6: utumno6 indexes a function-pointer table with a signed value: index -1 writes attacker-controlled data over a GOT/pointer entry.
goals.7: utumno7's vuln() strcpy()s argv[1] into a stack buffer; the return address is overwritten at ~140 bytes.
goals.8: Final account: log in as utumno8 and read the CONGRATULATIONS file.

cmds: # utumno0 is execute-only: strings/objdump/readelf all refuse it
ls -l /utumno/utumno0
strings /utumno/utumno0
objdump -d /utumno/utumno0
/utumno/utumno0 < /dev/null
# LD_PRELOAD a 32-bit constructor dumper: read /proc/self/maps, dump the binary's own mappings
# compile 32-bit and load it, then treat the dump as an ordinary binary
objdump -d -M intel /tmp/utumno0.dump | sed -n '/<main>:/,/^$/p'
# the binary mmaps an RWX page, copies a string into it and calls it
file /utumno/utumno1
objdump -d -M intel /utumno/utumno1 | sed -n '/<main>:/,/^$/p'
readelf -lW /utumno/utumno1 | grep GNU_STACK
cat /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space
# write the shellcode in vim: no NUL bytes, no slashes, builds /bin/sh byte by byte
nasm -f elf32 l1.asm -o l1.o
objcopy -O binary --only-section=.text l1.o l1.bin
xxd -p l1.bin
# build the file name (sh_ + shellcode) and run it
levels.note: the shellcode runs from the RWX page and prints the password file

cmds: /utumno/utumno2 </dev/null
/utumno/utumno2 AAAA </dev/null
# both refuse: the guard wants argc == 1 and an empty argv[0]
objdump -d -M intel /utumno/utumno2 | sed -n '/<main>:/,/^$/p'
# with one argument, argv[10] is envp[8] — the payload rides there
# write the shellcode in vim, drive it from ctypes with an empty argv[0]
# sweep for a working return address, re-run the hit with shell commands
# loop: index = getchar() ^ 3*k, value = getchar(), buffer[index] = value
# index is a signed char used as an offset — it can go negative and past the buffer
objdump -d -M intel /utumno/utumno3 | sed -n '/<main>:/,/^$/p'
# confirm the arithmetic in gdb, choose the shellcode location
# write the shellcode in vim, build the exploit in vim
# sweep the return address, re-run the hit
levels.note: the signed-char write redirects the return address to shellcode in argv[0]

cmds: /utumno/utumno4 </dev/null
# segfault with no args — the interesting path needs arguments
objdump -d -M intel /utumno/utumno4 | sed -n '/<main>:/,/^$/p'
# the guard reads only a WORD (16 bits) of the length; memcpy uses the DWORD
readelf -lW /utumno/utumno4 | grep GNU_STACK
cat /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space
# buf = ebp-0xff02, return address at offset 0xff06 = 65286
# len = 65536 + 63 = 65599 passes the guard and reaches the return address
# write the shellcode in vim, build the exploit in vim, run it
# same argc/argv guard as utumno2; argv[10] is envp[8]
objdump -d -M intel /utumno/utumno5 | sed -n '/<main>:/,/^$/p'
# hihi: strings longer than 0x13 are strncpy-capped at 20 bytes
# the return address is overwritten, but the shellcode stays in envp[8]
# write the shellcode in vim, build the exploit in vim
# sweep the return address, re-run the hit
levels.note: strncpy caps long strings at 20 bytes: ret is overwritten, shellcode stays in envp[8]

cmds: /utumno/utumno6
/utumno/utumno6 1 deadbeef hello
# the bounds check is signed: (int)pos > 0xa — but pos is used as a full 32-bit index
objdump -d -M intel /utumno/utumno6 | sed -n '/<main>:/,/^$/p'
# pos = 4294967295 (-1) passes the check and rewrites the strcpy destination pointer
/utumno/utumno6 4294967295 41414141 BBBB
# measure the layout in gdb, write the shellcode and the exploit in vim, run it
/utumno/utumno7
/utumno/utumno7 AAAA
